study.title: Isaiah 26 - Song of trust, judgment, and final hope
study.overview: Isaiah 26 presents a song of praise and trust that celebrates the security that God gives to his people, the humiliation of proud powers, the persevering waiting of the righteous in the midst of oppression and the hope of resurrection and final judgment. The chapter alternates between triumph, prayer and mourning, but converges to the certainty that the Lord rules history, corrects wickedness and preserves his people until the final restoration.

outline.title: The strong city and the path of the righteous
outline.explanation: The first verses describe the community of God as a city protected by the salvation of the Lord. The entrance is given to the righteous and faithful nation, and complete peace is promised to him who trusts in God. In contrast, the mighty arrogant are slaughtered, while the way of the righteous is straightened by God Himself.

outline.title: Desire for justice, recognition of discipline and memory of God's action
outline.explanation: From here the voice of the community expresses desire for the presence and judgments of God. The text recognizes that the wicked do not learn justice or when they receive favor. Then the people confess that the hand of God weighs on history, that peace comes from him and that even the good deeds of the people proceed from the Lord, who humiliates other lords and magnifies his nation.

outline.title: distress, hope of resurrection and judgment on earth
outline.explanation: The final section recalls the pain of the people under discipline, compared to the pains of childbirth, and admits that their efforts did not produce liberation for themselves. Then hope rises: the dead of the Lord will live, and the people must gather until wrath passes. The chapter ends with the certainty that God will go out to punish wickedness and reveal the hidden crimes of the earth.

study.context: The notes describe this chapter as a song of praise and prayer for redemption. Tyndale places him in the part called the "Small" apocalypse" of Isaiah, as a celebration of the restoration of the people of God. Matthew Henry notes that the song should be prepared to be sung when the promise is fulfilled. Adam Clarke also understands him as a hymn of thanksgiving, with contrast between the city protected by God and the enemies of the slaughtered enemy powers. The notes also mention that, in time of anguish, the people seek God under discipline, and that the final hope includes the resurrection.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the true security of God's people is not in human fortifications, but in the salvation that the Lord himself places as a wall. Justice and faithfulness are the hallmarks of the citizens of the city of God, and complete peace is linked to persevering trust. Also appears divine sovereignty over history: God overthrows pride, disciplines his people, sustains the righteous, and judges the wicked. Theologically, the text unites providence, holiness and eschatological hope. Affliction is not denied, but is read in the light of God's action. The chapter culminates in the hope of the resurrection of the Lord's dead and in the final judgment that exposes hidden wickedness. Confessional Christian reading can see in these images anticipations of God's final victory over evil and the full restoration of his people, without reducing the text only to an immediate historical event.

scholarViews.insight: The city of God is the sure community of the Lord; its walls are salvation, and there is no ultimate danger against his people.
The chapter summons the people of God to trust in the Lord forever, because he humbles the proud and sustains those who humble themselves.
The verse points to the hope of the resurrection, linked to the deliverance of the people of God from their lowest condition.

questions: In which areas of life do I still seek security in human walls, rather than trust in the salvation of the Lord?
Has the discipline of God led me to prayer and to the learning of justice, or only to inner resistance?
How does the hope of the resurrection and final judgment change the way in which it faces present injustices?
study.practice: Practice trusting in God in a concrete way: when facing fear, injustice or anxiety, transform the immediate reaction into prayer; recognize daily that peace comes from the Lord; and examine whether your actions have produced justice and fidelity or only fruitless effort. It is also worth cultivating perseverance: waiting in God is not passivity, but to continue seeking his way until he reveals his righteousness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow us to safely determine whether the chapter refers mainly to a specific historical moment, although they mention the anguish of the people in the time of Hezekiah as possible illustration. Nor is it possible to affirm, only with these notes, to what extent each image should be read first as an immediate reference to Israel/Juda or as the broader typology of the church and the final consummation. The interpretations of resurrection and city of God are presented in the notes as interpretive readings, not as a single and undeniable definition of the text.
